changes: Apartment buildings often refer to acoustic standards when determining which flooring options are acceptable. Two common measurements are the Impact Insulation Class (IIC) and the Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC). Understanding these helps you choose the appropriate underlay and hybrid flooring product.

Acoustic reports may describe different products, floor constructions and test conditions. Ask for the full report for the proposed flooring system and confirm which requirements and approval process apply to your building before comparing isolated figures.
IIC measures how well flooring reduces impact noise. Higher numbers indicate better performance. Many Sydney apartment buildings require a minimum IIC rating for new floor installations.

If an acoustic report cites IIC, ask which floor construction, product, underlay and test conditions it covers. Confirm whether that report and any required rating are accepted for your building; do not assume a generic minimum applies to every Sydney apartment.
NRC measures how well a material absorbs sound. Underlays with higher NRC values help soften footfall and reduce echo within the apartment itself.

Confirm the relevance of any NRC figure with the building's acoustic adviser before using it to compare flooring. Do not assume that a single figure demonstrates compliance; request the relevant floor-system report and written approval requirements.
Even if your hybrid flooring includes an attached acoustic layer, strata bylaws may require a specific underlay type or thickness. Select an option that meets or exceeds your building requirements.

Before choosing a separate underlay, check the exact hybrid product's installation instructions, attached backing and permitted floor-system build-up. Confirm the proposed system with the building's approval process; do not assume that adding underlay establishes compliance.

changes: Floor levelling isn’t just about fixing visible imperfections like cracks or stains on your property’s flooring. It’s about creating a solid and level base for your timber floors. If your underlying concrete slab isn’t flat and smooth, your timber floors could face issues down the road, which could cost you more.

Floor levelling addresses localised surface variation before flooring installation. Review the exposed substrate, moisture and movement concerns before choosing a preparation method. A floor can slope and still be flat; the selected product's requirements determine the preparation needed.
Without it, you risk structural issues, increased wear and tear, and reduced aesthetic appeal.
Preparation should be reviewed for the selected product. Structural movement, active cracking and moisture problems may need separate investigation rather than surface levelling alone.
